head.h11: What it does, and what it doesn't
head.p2: Every number here came out of code in the public repository, and the failures are on this page next to the successes. A result that goes the wrong way is still a result; the point of the project is what the connectome can do, not what we can script it into doing.

s1.p2: The fly's senses are fed the game; its descending neurons press the buttons. The brain itself is never trained — only the encoder going in and the readout coming out.
s1.h31: It chases, and it chases for the right reason
s1.p3: Against a scripted dummy for 90 seconds, 64% of its moves went toward the opponent, where chance is 50%. The pathway doing it is LC10a → DNa02 — the same circuit a male fly uses to chase a mate. With eight copies of the brain voting, that rises to 72% (against 63% for a single fly), with far fewer random moves.
s1.p4: 22% of its jumps happened while a projectile was nearby, against 20% for random jumping. That is chance. The escape pathway fires, but nothing has taught it when to use it.
s1.h33: The readouts, against a baseline that sees the game directly
s1.p5: A linear readout is trained on recorded matches to predict whether a press will connect, then scored on held-out matches. The honest comparison is a baseline that just looks at the distance between the fighters — information the fly does not get cleanly.
s1.p6: At its chosen threshold the punch readout presses on 9% of chances and 19% of those connect, against 10% for random presses — but a one-line “punch when in reach” rule presses on 8% of chances and connects 50% of the time. The fly loses to the rule. We do not use the rule: a win from scripted rules would tell us nothing about the connectome.
s1.h34: Tuning the encoder, not the brain
s1.p7: Searching how the game reaches the looming neurons moved the punch readout from AUC 0.685 (hand-set) to 0.789 (looming scaled by size 0.6), replicated across three runs and flat up to 1.2 before collapsing at 1.8. The distance-only baseline still wins at 0.867. The interface, not the wiring, is the bottleneck — which is why the roadmap learns the interface first and treats wiring edits as a separate experiment.
s1.h35: It was thinking two frames late, and fixing that won a match
s1.p8: Eight voting copies of the brain took 59–70 ms per frame in a game that gives you 33 ms. Two copies take 16–27 ms, and with the same encoder and readout the fly won its first match, 100–67 and 61–15. On recordings made with the tuned encoder, the trained punch readout reaches AUC 0.863, against 0.890 for the distance baseline, so the gap nearly closed.

s2.h21: A fly's alarm call reaches another fly
s2.p2: Two copies of the connectome. One lives through a situation, and its wing motor neurons sing. The other hears the song through its own ear neurons. Nothing between them is scripted, and the tests were fixed before any run.
s2.td1: Song carries what happened to the singer
s2.td3: Listener reacts to a threat song, vs silence
s2.p3: Threat is the clear word in every run, and a mate in view becomes partly readable at 2 ms. The listener's brain carries the singer's situation in every run and stays at chance in silence. Fixing the smell neurons — they were exciting each other into a runaway loop — lets a food odour reach the brain.
s2.a1: Read the full experiment and the feed

s3.h21: Flies that forage, mate and die
s3.p2: A second model, smaller and built to the same block diagram: 748 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons per fly, 5,716 synapses, and one part that learns: a mushroom body. Because every fly is cheap, whole pathways can be cut and the population measured with and without them.
s3.h31: Cast-and-surge falls out of the wiring
s3.p3: 16 flies, wind 1.6 m/s, 180 s, binned by how long it has been since a puff of odour hit:
s3.p4: Monotonic in all four columns: on contact a fly speeds up, straightens, heads further upwind and drives its wings harder; as the plume is lost it slows, turns more and drifts off the wind axis. That is textbook surge-and-cast, and nothing in the code says to do it. It falls out of receptors that report the onset of a puff feeding the same steering and thrust populations the wind pathway feeds.
s3.h32: The escape reflex is worth something under predation
s3.p5: Spiders rear up — which the eyes see as real looming — and strike. 24 flies, 250 s, four independent world seeds. Deaths are per 1,000 fly-seconds, so a run that loses flies early is not scored as safer.
s3.p6: Cutting the looming input raises deaths 6.5×, but it also parks the flies near the ground, so most of that is posture rather than a failed escape. Cutting the giant fibre's output is the clean test: the neuron still fires, time near the ground is unchanged, and deaths still more than double. That is the escape circuit doing its job, measured with the confound removed.
s3.h33: A memory for smells, and a world that never stops
s3.p7: Every fly now has a mushroom body. Kenyon cells give each smell its own sparse signature: over a quarter of them fire for a given odour, and fruit, carrion and mouldy fruit come out clearly different. Dopamine neurons are wired to the fly's own senses (a looming threat, a knock, alarm CO<sub>2</sub>, a taste of juice) and, only when they burst, weaken the synapses of whatever smell was present.
s3.td6: Is the smell code sparse and odour-specific?
s3.td8: Does punishment write a memory of that smell, and only that one?
s3.td9: Yes: its pull drops from 1.16 to 0.06 Hz; exposure alone leaves it alone
s3.td11: Not measurably yet: the memory barely reaches the wings
s3.td12: Can a fly learn a smell from another fly’s fright?
s3.td13: No: onlookers learn from seeing the threat themselves
s3.p8: Every test had its pass mark written before it ran, and all four rounds are in the world README. The world itself now runs around the clock on a server and records every mating, egg, meal, death, family tree and relationship, with a live report and CSV exports.
s3.p9: Cut the descending neurons off the premotor pool and the flies stop being flies: wing motor 7.4 → 2.5 Hz, speed 1.89 → 0.07 m/s, altitude 3.51 → 0.42 m. They sit on the ground twitching. Cut the ventral optic-flow cells instead and altitude collapses from 3.5 m to 0.89 m — height in this model is held by the same optic-flow loop insects use, not by a controller.

s4.p2: The geosmin pathway — the labelled line a real fly uses to avoid mould — is wired in and it fires: the receptor runs at 1.6 Hz and the lateral horn at 6.5–9 Hz next to mouldy fruit. But the flies do not avoid the mould. In a two-choice arena the side-swap variance is larger than any ablation effect. The aversive signal reaches steering at a few Hz against a much larger arousal background, and it loses.
s4.h32: The aggregation pheromone does not attract
s4.p3: Flies looked like they clustered around each other. Measured speed-independently — is a fly heading at its nearest neighbour? — the effect is −0.049 intact and −0.000 with the pheromone cut. The clustering was arousal, not attraction. The original result did not survive a better measurement.
s4.h33: Smell does not win foraging in a crowd
s4.p4: Cutting the food odour channel entirely changes mean distance to fruit from 11.37 m to 11.21 m. In a 32 m field with dozens of food sources, where flies settle dominates what they search for. Surge is real and measurable; it just does not show up in this particular metric.
s4.h34: The courtship circuit does not decide who mates
s4.p5: The male command neuron P1 and the song command pIP10 are wired in and respond to their inputs: cutting the visual input drops P1 from 5.1 Hz to 1.8 Hz, cutting the contact input pushes it to 11.3 Hz. Across that six-fold range, the number of matings does not change — 6.0 ± 1.6 intact, and every ablation overlaps it. Mating in the simulation is proximity plus a threshold, not courtship. The circuit is real; our use of it was not.
s4.h35: Scrambled wiring talks too, at 2 ms
s4.p6: At 20 ms, a brain with the same neurons but scrambled connections sang nothing useful (0.01 bits). At 2 ms its song carries 0.87 bits, as much as the real brain's 0.83, so the test we set for “the real wiring matters” fails there. The two brains group the situations differently, but we only noticed that after seeing the data.
s4.h36: Smell reaches the brain but not the wings
s4.p7: With the smell loop fixed, a food odour drives the fly's odour relay neurons at 125 Hz, against 4 Hz without it. The signal then never reaches the wing motor neurons, so a food song looks the same as no song, and listeners ignore it.
s4.h37: A caveat that applies to every ablation above
s4.p8: Each neuron's incoming weights are normalised to sum to 1, so cutting one input raises the weight of the rest. These are not clean knockouts, and small differences between rows should not be trusted. Stated here rather than buried, because it limits every table on this page.

s5.li1: The wiring is real; the neurons are simplified. One simple model per cell, no dendrites, no neuromodulators. The only learning is the 3-D world's small mushroom body.
s5.li2: The 3-D world is not the connectome: 748 neurons against 166,700, with real cell-type names but invented counts and weights.
s5.li3: The eye is a shortcut. Signals are fed into the fly's motion-detecting neurons rather than simulating its optics.
s5.li4: Which neurons press which game buttons was chosen by us.
s5.li5: Flybook's words are a decoder's labels for measured wing activity, with the decoder's accuracy shown on every post. The flies have two words, not a language.
